How are you ripping me off without me knowing it?

• FINANCING - if you let me find your financing, I'll get a kick-back (aka "Dealer Participation") from the bank - the higher the interest rate I give you, the higher the kick-back
  • DOCUMENT FEE - random fee, meaningless, can be negotiated out of a deal every time
  • GAP PROTECTION - waste of money for you, highly profitable for me
  • SERVICE CONTRACT - see above
So say you're in my shoes. How do you negotiate with another salesman like yourself? What would you do to ensure you're the one getting a good deal?

Shop around - know the prices of similar vehicles being sold at the dealer's competitors. Don't be afraid to make a low offer - salesman will never walk away from an offer. Offer low, stick with it, and be willing to leave when the salesman says no. Wait for the salesman to call you back.

Educate yourself - dealers base pricing on NADA guides. Generally we buy cars for "Trade In Average" and sell them at "Clean Retail". A "good deal" is a car that's in great condition, with a clean history, has new tires, comes with a reasonable warranty, and is priced somewhere between those two numbers.

Ridiculously competitive. Just in the 10 years that I've been in business, I've seen huge changes in that regard. New car dealers entering the used car market, major increases in used car exporting, internet advertising expanding the market range of your competition, etc. It's a very cut-throat business - very difficult to make good money.

If someone walks in, offers a little more than what you paid for the car (take it or leave it). Is that person seen as a quick commission or just someone to rush out of the door to make space for for "real commissions"?

I run two smaller lots - neither have salesman that work on commission, so I can't really give a good answer to that question. I will say this much, I will only sell a vehicle at or near cost if it is a "problem car" - one that has condition issues and/or has been sitting on my lot for a long time
Do you have any tips for people looking to buy used cars that have no negotiating and/or mechanic skills to avoid being taken to the cleaners?

Yes. Find your own financing. Take the vehicle to a reputable mechanic to have it inspected. Use NADA guides for yoru pricing - you should never pay more than 90% of NADA Clean Retail. Don't let the dealer up-sell you - service contracts are junk, GAP protection isn't worth it, etc. Ask the dealer if you can see their inspection/repair sheet for the vehicle. Get a vehicle history report. Know whether the vehicle is equipped with a timing belt, and if that timing belt has been or needs to be serviced. Don't pay a doc fee. Set a price you're willing to pay (say for instance, 90% of NADA Clean Retail) and be willing to walk away
Thank you. Now what is a doc fee?
Document fee - an extra fee that dealers add on after the price is negotiated, typically a couple hundred dollars. It's generally not spoken of, but inserted in your Bill of Sale.
What are tips or tricks from buying cars from craigslist/autotrader that people may not be aware of? Also, what is the most common scam you've run across?

If you are buying private party, only purchase one-owner vehicles. Get your vehicle history report (save some money and get the Autocheck report, instead of the CarFax) so you can verify that it is a one-owner.

It's not about economic difficulties; on that front, Europe is doing at least tolerably by most measures. It's about the idea of European unity. Politically, Euroskepticism is on the rise, and the problems with Greece are heavily reinforcing the simmering idea that there is no such thing as "one European people." The rhetoric is now all about the Germans vs. the Greeks, or the creditor countries vs. the lender countries, or everyone vs. Greece.

These rifts show little hope of closing, as there are few ways out of the crisis from here. Functionally, either Greece must leave the Eurozone, which would send an irreversible message that the union is not permanent, or the ECB must relent and forgive Greek debts, which would have richer countries out for blood because their money just vanished, and debtor countries outraged because Greece is getting special treatment. This would also further increase the growing rift between Europeans.

The way I see it, no matter which of these routes is taken, it will be enough to fan the flames of dissent such that one country will leave the EU, probably the UK, and once that happens the EU is doomed. All it takes is one thread pulled out for the whole tapestry to unravel.
